literal: His son Hui, styled Xianshun.
idiomatic: His son Hui, styled Xianshun.

literal: He had a rough acquaintance with books and histories and considerable talent for administration.
idiomatic: He had dipped into histories and showed real talent for office.

literal: In Shizong's time he inherited the fief.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he inherited the fief.

literal: He was made General of Raiding Cavalry and went out as Administrator of Henei.
idiomatic: He was named general of raiding cavalry and Henei administrator.

literal: In the commandery he was pure and orderly and had a reputation among the people.
idiomatic: In the commandery he ruled cleanly and won the people's praise.

literal: He was summoned and appointed Acting Regular Attendant Cavalier in Ordinary Service.
idiomatic: He was recalled as acting regular attendant cavalier in ordinary service.

literal: In Suzong's time he was made General of the Right and Inspector of Liangzhou.
idiomatic: Under Suzong he became general of the right and Liangzhou inspector.

literal: Hui, because the route was long and obstructed, firmly requested not to go.
idiomatic: The road to Liangzhou was long and hard; Hui begged off.

literal: He was made Regular Attendant Cavalier in Ordinary Service.
idiomatic: He was made regular attendant cavalier in ordinary service.

literal: That same year he was made General of the Rear and Inspector of Bingzhou.
idiomatic: That year he was named general of the rear and Bingzhou inspector.

literal: Earlier, within the province's borders there had been summer frost; the grain did not ripen; the people fled and scattered, and few kept to their livelihood.
idiomatic: Earlier summer frost had struck the province, crops failed, people fled, and few could keep their fields.

literal: Hui at once opened the granaries to relieve them; civil and military officials alike remonstrated to stop him.
idiomatic: Hui opened the granaries at once; civil and military officers alike tried to stop him.

literal: Hui said: "In the past Ji Changru, though only a commandery administrator, still opened the granaries to save the people from disaster and hardship—how much more I, close kin of the imperial house, entrusted with a great frontier, can I cling to the law and not rescue the people's distress?
idiomatic: Hui said: "Ji Changru was only a commandery chief yet opened the granaries in famine—how can a prince of the blood, entrusted with a great frontier, cling to statute and let the people starve?"

literal: " He distributed first and memorialized afterward.
idiomatic: He gave grain first and reported afterward.

literal: Suzong praised him.
idiomatic: Suzong praised him.

literal: He was added as General Who Pacifies the North.
idiomatic: He was also named general who pacifies the north.

literal: Later he was made General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Qinzhou.
idiomatic: Later he was made general who pacifies the west and Qinzhou inspector.

literal: The edict arrived in the morning and he set out the same evening.
idiomatic: The edict came at dawn and he left that evening.

literal: Hui, because he was about to go to the Qin region, requested to come to court to receive the appointment with ceremony and repeatedly memorialized, firmly asking not to take the post.
idiomatic: Bound for Qin, he asked to receive the seal at court and memorialized again and again to decline the post.

literal: He was changed to General Who Assists the State, added as Director of the Department of Revenue in the Masters of Writing, and advanced in title to General Who Stabilizes the Army.
idiomatic: He was shifted to general who assists the state, made director of revenue in the masters of writing, and promoted to general who stabilizes the army.

literal: At that time war-horses were at the suburbs and the royal army had repeatedly been defeated; Hui, for military expenses, presented from his fief two thousand bolts of silk and ten thousand shi of grain to aid the army.
idiomatic: War had reached the suburbs and the royal army kept losing; Hui gave two thousand bolts of silk and ten thousand shi of grain from his fief for the campaign.

literal: Suzong did not accept.
idiomatic: Suzong refused the gift.

literal: He was also made concurrently Director of Personnel in the Masters of Writing, added as Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Pacifies the East, and transferred to General of the Guard and Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
idiomatic: He also held personnel in the masters of writing, attendant-in-ordinary, general who pacifies the east, then general of the guard and right grand master of splendid happiness.

literal: He was made Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, then transferred to General of Chariots and Cavalry with Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes; he firmly declined and would not accept; only after he was allowed to resign Attendant-in-Ordinary did he then accept the edict.
idiomatic: He was made left vice director of the masters of writing, then general of chariots and cavalry with equal honor to the three dukes; he refused until allowed to shed attendant-in-ordinary, then accepted.

literal: Soon he was made Director of the Masters of Writing, added Opening of the Office and Western Circuit Touring Secretariat; he did not go.
idiomatic: Soon he was director of the masters of writing with opening of the office and western touring secretariat, but would not take the field post.

literal: At that time Empress Dowager Ling held sole power and court discipline collapsed.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling ruled alone and court discipline rotted.

literal: Hui, though he held favored trust, offered no correction; with Zheng Yan and his sort he vied in forming factions.
idiomatic: Though favored, Hui corrected nothing; he and Zheng Yan's circle traded factions.

literal: Outwardly he seemed gentle and cautious; inwardly he was full of suspicion; the smallest grudge he was sure to repay.
idiomatic: Outwardly mild, inwardly suspicious, he repaid every slight.

literal: Men of insight despised him.
idiomatic: Knowing men despised him.

literal: He also could not restrain his wife, the Lady Yu, who then had an affair with Prince Yuan of Guangyang.
idiomatic: He could not restrain his wife Lady Yu, who took Prince Yuan of Guangyang as lover.

literal: When Yuan took command of the military headquarters, in every memorial he discussed Hui's faults; though it involved slander, much of it was true.
idiomatic: When Yuan commanded the army staff, every memorial denounced Hui; much of the slander was true.

literal: When Emperor Xiaozhuang ascended the throne, Hui was made Governor of Sizhou; soon he was made Minister of Education while still holding the governorship.
idiomatic: When Xiaozhuang took the throne, Hui became Sizhou governor, then minister of education while keeping the governorship.

literal: When Yuan Hao entered Luoyang, Hui followed Emperor Xiaozhuang on the northern tour; when the imperial carriage returned to the palace, for his merit in the plot he was made Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Marshal, Grand Duke, with feather canopy and martial music, and his fief was increased to twenty thousand households in all with the rest of his offices as before.
idiomatic: When Yuan Hao took Luoyang, Hui followed Xiaozhuang north; on the return, for the plot's merit he was attendant-in-ordinary, grand marshal, and grand duke with canopy and martial music, his fief raised to twenty thousand households, other ranks unchanged.

literal: Hui memorialized to decline offices and fiefs, repeatedly submitting.
idiomatic: Hui memorialized to decline rank and fief again and again.

literal: He also memorialized, saying: "The merit on the river was the soldiers' doing; I ask to return what was enfeoffed and add it to the meritorious."
idiomatic: He also wrote: "The victory on the river belonged to the soldiers; return my fief to them."

literal: Hui was personally favored by Emperor Xiaozhuang; inwardly he feared excessive honor, and therefore made this declination to guard against outside criticism.
idiomatic: Xiaozhuang favored him; fearing excess honor, he declined to blunt gossip.

literal: Emperor Xiaozhuang understood his intent and allowed him to decline the fief but did not permit him to yield the offices.
idiomatic: Xiaozhuang saw through him, let the fief go, and kept the offices.

literal: Hui's later wife was the emperor's cousin by marriage.
idiomatic: Hui's second wife was the emperor's cousin by marriage.

literal: Attendant-in-Ordinary Li Yu was the emperor's brother-in-law.
idiomatic: Attendant-in-Ordinary Li Yu was the emperor's brother-in-law.

literal: Hui's nature was fawning and ingratiating; he was skilled at winning favor for himself; relying on inside and outside connections, among the imperial clan and kin none could compare with him.
idiomatic: Fawning and skilled at currying favor, he used court and clan ties as no other prince could match.

literal: Then together with Yu and the others he urged the emperor to plot against Rong; Emperor Xiaozhuang too had long harbored the intent.
idiomatic: With Yu and the rest he urged the emperor to move against Rong; Xiaozhuang had long meant to.

literal: When Rong died, Shilong and the others held their positions and would not disband.
idiomatic: After Rong's death Shilong's faction held together and would not disperse.

literal: Hui was made Grand Guardian while still Grand Marshal, Imperial Clan Mentor, and Recorder of Affairs for the Masters of Writing, presiding over inner and outer affairs.
idiomatic: Hui was made grand guardian while keeping grand marshal, imperial clan mentor, and recorder of the masters of writing, commanding court and camp.

literal: Hui had originally supposed that after Rong's death the branches would naturally scatter and perish.
idiomatic: He had assumed Rong's kin would scatter once Rong was dead.

literal: When the Erzhu clan gathered and plotted trouble, Hui's stratagems had no outcome—only fear.
idiomatic: When the Erzhu clan gathered to rebel, Hui had no plan—only fear.

literal: By nature he was full of jealousy and did not wish anyone to stand before him.
idiomatic: Jealous by nature, he would brook no one ahead of him.

literal: Whenever he entered to discuss plans, he alone decided with the emperor.
idiomatic: In council he alone decided with the emperor.

literal: When court ministers submitted military and state strategy, he all urged the emperor not to accept it, saying petty bandits were nothing to worry about eliminating.
idiomatic: When ministers offered strategy, he told the emperor to reject it, calling the Erzhu a trifle easily crushed.

literal: He was also stingy with wealth, both for his household and for the state.
idiomatic: He was miserly with his own purse and the state's alike.

literal: Therefore whenever there were rewards and gifts, they were all meager, or if large they were cut midway, or given and then pursued for return.
idiomatic: Rewards were always thin, or large gifts halved, or granted and then clawed back.

literal: There was only waste in expenditure, and kindness did not move men's hearts.
idiomatic: Money was wasted yet gratitude never followed.

literal: Emperor Xiaozhuang by nature was himself frugal and narrow; Hui above all supported this.
idiomatic: Xiaozhuang was frugal by nature, and Hui above all encouraged it.

literal: Junior Director of the Imperial Treasury Li Miao had been Hui's vice director when he was Minister of Education; Hui treated him quite generously.
idiomatic: Li Miao of the imperial treasury had been Hui's vice director when he was minister of education; Hui treated him well.

literal: Miao often offered loyal words; once Hui had his wish, he mostly did not adopt them.
idiomatic: Miao often spoke plainly; once Hui had power, he seldom listened.

literal: Miao said to others: "The Prince of Chengyang was born with bee eyes—and now the jackal's voice is about to show."
idiomatic: Miao told others: "The prince of Chengyang was born with bee eyes—and now the jackal's howl is coming."

literal: When Erzhu Zhao entered the city, the palace guards fled in disorder; Emperor Xiaozhuang walked out through the Cloud Dragon Gate.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Zhao entered Luoyang the guards broke; Xiaozhuang walked out the Cloud Dragon Gate.

literal: Hui mounted his horse and galloped across; the emperor repeatedly called to him, but Hui paid no heed and left.
idiomatic: Hui spurred his horse across; the emperor called again and again, but Hui would not turn back.

literal: He then fled south of the mountains to the house of his former clerk Kou Mi.
idiomatic: He fled south of the mountains to his old clerk Kou Mi's house.

literal: Mi outwardly received him but inwardly was ill at ease; he frightened Hui, saying officials were coming to seize him, and told him to hide elsewhere.
idiomatic: Mi sheltered him outwardly but inwardly feared him; he terrified Hui with word that arrest was near and sent him elsewhere.

literal: He had men waylay and kill him on the road and sent the corpse to Erzhu Zhao.
idiomatic: He had men ambush and kill him on the road and sent the body to Erzhu Zhao.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously given Bearer of the Staff, Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Preceptor, Grand Marshal, Recorder of Affairs for the Masters of Writing, and Governor of Sizhou; posthumous title: Wenxian.
idiomatic: Early in the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously bearer of the staff, attendant-in-ordinary, grand preceptor, grand marshal, recorder of the masters of writing, and Sizhou governor, styled Wenxian.

literal: His son Yan inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Yan succeeded.

literal: At the end of Wuding he reached the post of Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
idiomatic: Late in Wuding he rose to junior mentor of the heir apparent.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi took the throne, enfeoffments were lowered by precedent.

literal: Hui's elder brother: Xianwei
idiomatic: Hui's elder brother: Xianwei

literal: Hui's elder brother Xianwei was Supervising Attendant and Aide of the Ministry of Education.
idiomatic: Hui's elder brother Xianwei was supervising attendant and aide of the ministry of education.

literal: He died; posthumously given General Who Assists the State and Inspector of Eastern Yuzhou.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously general who assists the state and Eastern Yuzhou inspector.

literal: Hui's second elder brother: Xiangong
idiomatic: Hui's second elder brother: Xiangong

literal: (Appended son: Yanzhao)
idiomatic: (Appended son: Yanzhao)

literal: Hui's second elder brother Xiangong, styled Huaizhong.
idiomatic: Hui's second elder brother Xiangong, styled Huaizhong.

literal: He was Vice Director of Yangzhou; for military merit he was enfeoffed as Marquis Who Founded the State of Pingyang with a fief of three hundred households.
idiomatic: He was Yangzhou vice director and, for military merit, founding marquis of Pingyang with three hundred households.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaozhuang's reign he was made General of the North Center and transferred to General of the Left and Inspector of Eastern Xuzhou.
idiomatic: Early in Xiaozhuang's reign he was general of the north center, then general of the left and Eastern Xuzhou inspector.

literal: He entered as General Who Pacifies the East and Grand Minister of Agriculture.
idiomatic: He came in as general who pacifies the east and grand minister of agriculture.

literal: Soon he was made General of the Central Army and Inspector of Jingzhou.
idiomatic: Soon he was general of the central army and Jingzhou inspector.

literal: After Emperor Xiaozhuang killed Erzhu Rong, Xiangong was made Bearer of the Staff, Commander of military affairs in Jin, Jian, and Nanfen provinces, General Who Pacifies the West, concurrent Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, Northwestern Circuit Touring Secretariat, and Inspector of Jinzhou.
idiomatic: After Xiaozhuang killed Erzhu Rong, Xiangong was bearer of the staff, commander of Jin, Jian, and Nanfen, general who pacifies the west, left vice director of the masters of writing, northwestern touring secretariat, and Jinzhou inspector.

literal: After Erzhu Zhao entered Luoyang he died at Jinyang.
idiomatic: After Erzhu Zhao took Luoyang he died at Jinyang.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously given General of the Guard and Inspector of Bingzhou; later posthumously given again as General of Chariots and Cavalry with Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes.
idiomatic: Early in the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously general of the guard and Bingzhou inspector; later also general of chariots and cavalry with equal honor to the three dukes.

literal: His son Yanzhao inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yanzhao succeeded.

literal: In the Wuding era he was Administrator of Yuyang.
idiomatic: Under Wuding he governed Yuyang.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi took the throne, enfeoffments were lowered by precedent.

literal: Xiangong's younger brother: Prince of Xiangcheng Xu
idiomatic: Xiangong's younger brother: Prince of Xiangcheng Xu

literal: Xiangong's younger brother Xu, styled Xianhe.
idiomatic: Xiangong's younger brother Xu, styled Xianhe.

literal: In Emperor Xiaozhuang's time he was enfeoffed as Prince of Xiangcheng commandery with a fief of a thousand households.
idiomatic: Under Xiaozhuang he was prince of Xiangcheng commandery with a thousand households.

literal: At the end of Wuding he reached the post of Grand Marshal.
idiomatic: Late in Wuding he rose to grand marshal.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: After Qi took the throne, enfeoffments were lowered by precedent.

literal: Prince Jing of Zhangwu Tailuo
idiomatic: Prince Jing of Zhangwu Tailuo

literal: Prince of Zhangwu Tailuo died in the second year of Huangxing.
idiomatic: Prince of Zhangwu Tailuo died in Huangxing year 2.

literal: Posthumously he was given General Who Pacifies the North and Prince of Zhangwu commandery; posthumous title: Jing.
idiomatic: Posthumously he was general who pacifies the north and prince of Zhangwu commandery, styled Jing.

literal: He had no son.
idiomatic: He left no heir.

literal: At the beginning of Gaozu's reign the second son of Prince Hui of Nan'an, Bin, was made his heir.
idiomatic: Early in Gaozu's reign Bin, second son of Prince Hui of Nan'an, was made his heir.

literal: Heir: Bin
idiomatic: Heir: Bin

literal: Bin, styled Bao'er, inherited the title.
idiomatic: Bin, styled Bao'er, succeeded.

literal: Brave and strong, with martial ability.
idiomatic: Brave and martial.

literal: He went out as Bearer of the Staff, Commander of military affairs in Eastern Qin, Bin, and Xia provinces, General Who Pacifies the West, Protector of the Western Rong, Grand General of Tongwan Garrison, and Inspector of Shuozhou.
idiomatic: He went out bearer of the staff, commander of Eastern Qin, Bin, and Xia, general who pacifies the west, protector of the western Rong, Tongwan garrison grand general, and Shuozhou inspector.

literal: [6] For greed his fief was reduced.
idiomatic: [6] Greed cost him part of his fief.

literal: At that time the Tujing Hu rebelled; an edict made Bin Bearer of the Staff, Acting General Who Pacifies the North, and Acting Commissioner for Bingzhou affairs; he led the forces of Bing and Si to attack them; when the Hu were pacified he was made General Who Punishes the Barbarians and Inspector of Fenzhou.
idiomatic: When the Tujing Hu rebelled, Bin was bearer of the staff, acting general who pacifies the north, and acting Fenzhou commissioner; he led Bing and Si troops to crush them, then was named general who punishes the barbarians and Fenzhou inspector.

literal: More than six hundred Hu households led by Quju and others held defiles and plotted rebellion, inciting their fellows.
idiomatic: More than six hundred Hu households under Quju held the passes and stirred their clans to revolt.

literal: Bin requested twenty thousand troops; the authorities memorialized approval.
idiomatic: Bin asked for twenty thousand men; the court approved.

literal: Gaozu was greatly angered and said: "How can there be reason to move troops and horses!
idiomatic: Gaozu raged: "What reason is there to march an army!"

literal: Deal with it as circumstances require; if you cannot by expedient means quiet and settle it, and a great force is truly needed, then first behead the inspector, and only then send out troops.
idiomatic: Quiet them by whatever means fit; if you cannot settle it without a host, behead the inspector first, then raise the army.
